King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

sess136.d: As computing demands surge for AI and HPC applications, networking becomes essential for performance and scaling. AI and HPC fabrics are used in scale-up and scale-out communications. This workshop will cover innovations in AI/HPC fabric architecture, network transport, load balancing, congestion control, network resilience, and network visibility. The workshop will further focus on Ethernet technologies for AI and HPC including Scale-Up Ethernet Transport (SUE-T), Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN), Ultra Ethernet, advanced congestion control, lossless transport mechanisms, telemetry, and fabric management.

sess130.d: Quantum computing is advancing rapidly, and its integration with high performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly important for enabling practical hybrid computational workflows. In a growing number of domains, research is progressing toward quantum advantage — with quantum computation already addressing problems that strain exact classical methods and increasingly competing with state-of-the-art approximate approaches. These combined methods offer new opportunities for accelerating progress in scientific areas such as physics, chemistry, materials, and optimization by leveraging quantum computing together with established classical and AI-based techniques. The 2nd Annual Workshop on Large-Scale Quantum-Classical Computing (LSQCC) brings together recent research on quantum algorithms, system integration techniques, and emerging hybrid workflows that incorporate HPC and AI components where beneficial. The workshop highlights technical challenges, recent developments, and near-term opportunities for effectively combining quantum computing with complementary approaches.

sess128.d: The ongoing revolution enabled via containerization, virtualization, and new orchestration models has dramatically changed how applications and services are delivered and managed across the computing industry. This revolution has established a new ecosystem of tools and techniques with new, flexible and agile approaches, and continues to gain traction in the HPC community. In addition to HPC-optimized container runtimes, technologies like Kubernetes create a new set of opportunities and challenges. While adoption is growing, questions regarding best practices, foundational concepts, tools, and standards remain. Our goal is to promote the adoption of these tools and introspect the impact of this new ecosystem on HPC/AI use cases. This workshop serves as a key venue for presenting late-breaking research, sharing experiences and best practices, and fostering collaboration in this field. Our eighth workshop iteration will continue to emphasize real-world experiences and challenges in adopting and optimizing these new approaches for HPC and AI.

sess131.d: Understanding program behavior is critical to overcome the expected architectural and programming complexities, such as limited power budgets, heterogeneity, hierarchical memories, shrinking I/O bandwidths, and performance variability, that arise on modern HPC platforms. To do so, HPC software developers need intuitive support tools for debugging, performance measurement, analysis, and tuning of large-scale HPC applications. Data collected from these tools can be far too large and too complex to be analyzed in a straightforward manner. We therefore need automatic analysis and visualization approaches to help application developers intuitively understand the effects that algorithmic choices have on application correctness or performance. The ProTools workshop brings together HPC application developers, tool developers, vendors, and researchers from the visualization, performance, and program analysis fields for an exchange of new approaches to assist developers in analyzing, understanding, and optimizing programs for extreme-scale platforms.

i: Erlangen National High Performance Computing Center

sess132.d: The complexity of high performance computing (HPC) systems necessitates advanced techniques in system administration, configuration, and engineering and with staff who are well-versed on the best practices in this field. HPC systems professionals include system engineers, system administrators, network administrators, storage administrators, and operations staff who face problems unique to HPC systems. The ACM SIGHPC SYSPROS Virtual Chapter, the sponsor for this workshop, has been established to provide opportunities to develop and grow relationships focused specifically on the needs of HPC systems practitioners and to act as a support resource for them to help with the issues encountered in this specialized field. This workshop is designed to share best practices for common HPC system deployment and maintenance, to provide a platform to discuss upcoming technologies, and to present the state-of-the-practice techniques that increase performance and reliability of systems, and in turn increase researcher and analyst productivity.

sess133.d: LLVM, winner of the 2012 ACM Software System Award, has become an integral part of the software-development ecosystem for optimizing compilers, dynamic-language execution engines, source-code analysis and transformation tools, debuggers and linkers and a whole host of programming-language and toolchain-related components. Now heavily used in both academia and industry, where it allows for rapid development of production-quality tools, LLVM is increasingly used in work targeted at high performance computing. Research in, and implementation of, program analysis, compilation, execution and profiling have clearly benefited from the availability of a high-quality, freely-available infrastructure on which to build. This workshop will focus on recent developments, from both academia and industry, that build on LLVM to advance the state of the art in high performance computing.

sess129.d: Efficient storage, movement, and management of data are crucial to application performance and scientific productivity in both traditional simulation-oriented HPC environments and cloud, AI/ML/big data analysis environments. This issue is further exacerbated by the growing volume of experimental and observational data, the widening gap between the performance of computational hardware and storage hardware, and the emergence of new data-driven algorithms in machine learning. The goal of this workshop is to facilitate in-depth discussions of research and development that address the most critical challenges in large-scale data storage and data processing. PDSW will continue to build on the successful tradition established by its predecessor workshops: the Petascale Data Storage Workshop (PDSW, 2006-2015) and the Data Intensive Scalable Computing Systems (DISCS, 2012-2015) workshop. These workshops were successfully combined in 2016, and the resulting joint workshop has attracted up to 45 full paper submissions and 195 attendees per year from 2016 to 2025.

sess127.d:
The WHPC@SC26 workshop will be held in Chicago, Illinois, USA, with the goal of fostering a diverse and inclusive HPC community. The WHPC workshop series has become the leading SC event focused on DEI topics. We aim to cultivate skills for valuing a diverse workforce and creating a welcoming environment for all. Following the workshop held at SC24, we have an increased emphasis on diversity and inclusion of all people from underrepresented groups.

WHPC@SC26 will focus on the following topics:
- Building community through real-time networking
- Improving diversity and inclusion for all in the HPC workforce
- Highlighting and supporting early-career researchers from underrepresented groups
- Building a deeper understanding of what diversity, equity, and inclusion means for different groups
- Learning from, and valuing, different experiences and career paths

sess188.d: Floating-point arithmetic is the bedrock of scientific computing, yet it frequently introduces subtle errors and non-deterministic behavior in numerical software. As the HPC community shifts toward mixed-precision execution to unlock performance and energy-efficiency gains, developers require robust methodologies to rigorously analyze floating-point error accumulation. This tutorial provides a comprehensive introduction to two state-of-the-art tools designed to guide precision-tuning decisions in both CPU and GPU-accelerated applications. The first tool is FPChecker, which leverages the Clang/LLVM compiler infrastructure to perform static and dynamic analysis of C/C++ applications. The second is NixNaN, a high-performance profiler built on the NVIDIA NVBit dynamic instrumentation framework, engineered to detect floating-point exceptional values arising during CUDA kernel execution without requiring source modification or recompilation. Throughout this session, participants will learn (1) to assess the floating-point dynamic range of applications, (2) to visualize the propagation of rounding errors, and (3) to isolate performance-critical numerical issues, such as overflows, and NaNs. The tutorial emphasizes a hands-on approach: attendees will engage with accessible examples (e.g., simple linear solvers) configured to run locally on their laptops. In the advanced session, we transition to real-world impact, where participants will apply these tools to larger numerical libraries (e.g., Hypre).

sess171.d: Integrating quantum resources into HPC workflows is complicated by two layers of fragmentation: quantum hardware vendors expose incompatible APIs, and HPC centers run diverse job schedulers. The Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI), an open-source project developed by a growing community of 15 national laboratories, institutions, and quantum vendors, resolves both problems by exposing quantum resources as first-class schedulable resources alongside CPUs and GPUs, independent of vendor or scheduler. This hands-on, three-hour tutorial targets HPC engineers and administrators, and gives quantum vendors concrete motivation: implement QRMI once, and your backend becomes accessible from any scheduler. The tutorial spans three modules covering today's HPC scheduling landscape: traditional batch schedulers, where attendees choose one of Slurm, PBS, IBM LSF, or Open Cluster Scheduler for hands-on exercises; Kubernetes, increasingly adopted for AI workloads; and the Flux Framework, a graph-based scheduler for next-generation HPC systems. In each module, participants submit real QRMI-managed jobs targeting cloud quantum resources from providers such as IBM, Pasqal, and Alice & Bob. Attendees will leave having experienced firsthand how QRMI integrates with their own workload manager to deliver quantum workloads to HPC users, giving them a concrete starting point for building quantum-ready HPC infrastructure today.

sess144.d: Heterogeneity is ubiquitous, not only in terms of processing units but also memories and networks. As heterogeneity increases, memory subsystems play an even more important role to attain performance, from their technology to the system architecture to the software management and programming model. While CPU-only compute nodes are becoming rare instances, heterogeneous memory architectures have recently emerged and revolutionized the traditional memory hierarchy. Today’s and upcoming architectures may well comprise multiple memory technologies next to DRAM, accelerators with dedicated memories, or even specific expansion cards hosting memory alone, such as: 3D-stacked memory, high-bandwidth multi-channel RAM, unified/shared memory on accelerators, Compute Express Link (CXL)-based architectures, Huawei's Unified Bus, persistent memory, or MRDIMMs.

sess141.d: How can AI workloads be engineered for optimal performance in modern HPC environments? As AI models grow in scale and complexity, high performance computing (HPC) systems are becoming essential for training and deploying these workloads. However, traditional HPC architectures, designed for batch processing, present unique challenges for AI/ML applications — such as dynamic workloads, high I/O demands, and parallelization intricacies. This workshop explores the intersection of AI and HPC, focusing on performance optimization, scalability, and portability. Topics include AI workload characterization, hybrid AI/HPC workflows, efficient execution strategies, and infrastructure co-design. By fostering collaboration between researchers, practitioners, and system developers, this workshop aims to advance best practices and innovations in AI-enabled scientific computing, aligning with SC26’s themes of exascale readiness and performance portability.

i: Norwegian University of Science and Technology

sess143.d: MPI is currently the de facto standard for programming HPC systems and developing parallel applications. Development of the MPI standard continues in earnest, with version 5.0 being released within the past year, and features for version 5.1d under active discussion. The aim of this workshop is to bring together researchers and developers to present and discuss innovative algorithms and concepts within the Message Passing programming model, and to create a forum for open discussions on the future of the Message Passing Interface (MPI) in the post-exascale era. Possible workshop topics include and are not limited to algorithms for collective operations, MPI optimization for artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads, data-centric models, scheduling, fault tolerance, MPI optimization in heterogeneous systems, interoperability of MPI with other programming models (e.g., PGAS), integration of task-parallel models in MPI, the role of MPI in "smart" networks, and the use of MPI in large-scale simulations.

i: Stony Brook University, Institute for Advanced Computational Science (IACS)

sess142.d: FTXS convenes researchers and practitioners to address trustworthy AI systems at scale under real-world variability. Modern AI/LLM pipelines (training, inference, RAG, and agentic systems) face “gray failures” such as distribution drift, prompt/tool/RAG variability, infrastructure noise, and limited-precision effects. Small perturbations can amplify into hallucinations, instability, miscalibration, irreproducibility, and silent regressions — wasting GPU-hours and undermining confidence in AI-assisted decisions. FTXS organizes discussion around a practical closed loop: Disturb → Degrade → Detect → Diagnose → Defend → Validate. We emphasize explainability as a diagnostic tool for attribution across components (model, retrieval, tools, infrastructure, precision), and we aim to synthesize shared taxonomies, measurement practices, and seed artifacts (checklists, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols) that improve both research and operational practice.

sess147.d: This workshop aims to bring together researchers, application scientists, system developers, and industry partners to explore algorithmic and implementation approaches enabling accurate scientific computing on low-precision hardware. As accelerators increasingly favor reduced-precision arithmetic for performance and energy efficiency, many scientific applications continue to require accuracy, stability, and reproducibility. Addressing this widening gap demands community-driven advances across algorithms and scientific software, spanning domain-informed and cross-cutting approaches while building toward reusable, precision-aware libraries and tooling infrastructure. The workshop will feature invited talks and solicited works highlighting mixed-precision methods, error-aware and adaptive numerical algorithms, floating-point emulation libraries, and practical deployment on large-scale systems. The workshop emphasizes building community-driven software ecosystems for broad adoption across domains, reducing duplication, and accelerating impact. By fostering discussion among application developers, numerical experts, and hardware vendors, the workshop will establish best practices, share lessons, and strengthen academia–industry collaboration to make low-precision hardware a reliable component of scientific workflows.

i: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Lincoln Laboratory

sess146.d: The Sixth International Symposium on Quantitative Co-Design of Supercomputers, or SQCS'26, considers combining two methodologies — collaborative co-design and data-driven analysis — to realize the potential of supercomputing more fully. By narrowing in on these two proven methodologies with the broad-community attention of an SC26 audience, we will address a host of identified challenges impacting high performance computing (HPC). The 2026 workshop focus will focus on upcoming machines and emerging technologies. The state of HPC is undergoing a fundamental transformation, moving beyond a sole focus on raw peak FLOPS (floating-point operations per second) to prioritizing time-to-solution, energy efficiency, and AI-simulation convergence. The landscape is defined by the rise of "post-exascale" machines, the integration of generative AI into scientific workflows, and the emergence of hybrid quantum-classical architectures. This symposium will bring together leaders in the field to review current efforts across centers and discuss areas that show potential.

sess145.d: Cancer touches everyone. Since being established in 2015, CAFCW continues to bring together the community interested in impacting cancer with HPC and the community with an interest in learning more about HPC impacting cancer challenges. The workshop continues to grow, inviting the cancer and HPC communities to converge at SC, interact, and share insights and advances. The workshop highlights the diversity of opportunities where HPC serves as an essential element for advances in cancer treatments, driving new approaches to understand cancer and enabling translation of insights and new treatments to reach clinical impact. This year, the workshop will emphasize the role of HPC in translating research to clinical application and reaching patients, uniting research, clinic and patient. For over a decade, this workshop has catalyzed new biomedical research by connecting industry, government research laboratories, and academia at the intersection of computation, biomedical science, cancer, and healthcare.

i: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
Institute for Data Science in Oncology
National Institutes of Health (NIH), National Cancer Institute (NCI)

sess246.d: AI is impacting all aspects of science. As the global scientific community embraces these tools and methods, we anticipate a potential acceleration of discovery in many areas. This prestigious international panel will discuss the implications for how we successfully harness the immense potential of AI.

i: European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking
National Supercomputing Centers in Shenzhen and Guangzhou

sess238.d: SCC Connect is a companion to the Student Cluster Competition (SCC) with a focus on accessibility and education. Using provided, cloud-based hardware, SCC Connect teams build and run benchmarks and a selection of real HPC workloads in a two-day nonstop competition. Teams compete remotely from all around the world, and several teams will attend SC26 and compete from booths in the Exhibit Hall. Come by to meet the teams and cheer them on!

sess501.d: Join this interactive, community-building experience by scanning your badge at the interactive kiosk, located in the Central Concourse, across from Registration. Using your registration details, we’ll generate a one-of-a-kind fractal image just for you — sent to you and showcased on displays throughout the conference. You’ll also appear on the HPC Around the World map, celebrating the global reach of high performance computing. Be sure to come back each day to generate a new image.

sess495.d:
Art of HPC

Where Creativity Meets HPC

Creativity has always been at the heart of innovation. It drives new perspectives, fuels artistic expression, and allows us to see beauty in unexpected places. By leveraging cutting-edge technology and resources, we can push the boundaries of both science and art. SC proudly presents Art of HPC, a showcase of the intersection between artistic creativity and high performance computing.

sess248.d: Scientific progress is limited not by a lack of new ideas but by the time and cost involved in physical experimentation. AI’s most transformative impact in enabling scientific discoveries lies in reducing the need for such experiments. To get there, we need to build AI models that are able to simulate and understand the physical world at all scales, which language models are unable to do. Neural operators lay the foundation for such multi-scale learning since they learn mappings between function spaces, and can accept inputs and outputs at any resolution. They have been successfully applied in weather and climate modeling, nuclear fusion, quantum chemistry, and designing novel medical devices. We are now bringing universality and scale, the key ingredients to the success of LLMs, to AI for physical understanding. I will share what we have already achieved and a glimpse of what lies ahead.

sess586.d: Ravi is a senior computer scientist working in the intersection of HPC/AI and biomedicine. His research interests are in building sustainable, scalable services for science, reproducible research, large-scale data management, analysis using HPC and AI. He leads the PALISADE-X project that is developing Privacy-preserving Federated Learning framework to build robust, trust-worthy AI models. He co-leads the MVP-CHAMPION project, which is a collaboration between VA and DOE and develops methods to perform large-scale genetic data analysis using DOE’s high performance computing capabilities, including methods for generating PRS scores in Prostate Cancer, genome-wide PheWAS on Summit supercomputer. Additionally, Ravi served as MPI for an NHGRI R01 on creating a cloud service for large-scale genomics analysis and was one of three key contributors to the National Institutes of Health $100M Cancer Biomedical Informatics Grid (caBIG), which linked 60 NIH-funded cancer centers and clinical sites engaged in cancer research. For his efforts in project management, tool development, and collaboration, Ravi received several Outstanding Achievement Awards from NIH. For his work on “Cancer Moonshot” project, he received the Department of Energy Secretary award in 2017.

i: Erlangen National High Performance Computing Center

sess239.d: SCC Connect is a companion to the Student Cluster Competition (SCC) with a focus on accessibility and education. Using provided, cloud-based hardware, SCC Connect teams build and run benchmarks and a selection of real HPC workloads in a two-day nonstop competition. Teams compete remotely from all around the world, and several teams will attend SC26 and compete from booths in the Exhibit Hall. Come by to meet the teams and cheer them on!

sess506.d: AI has had a profound impact on the supercomputing ecosystem, with dramatic advances in technology, size, and scale of supercomputers being deployed. While there is no doubt that AI software is very different from scientific computing applications, underneath the software, how different are the supercomputers powering the AI revolution? Have AI workloads fundamentally changed the technology used to build supercomputers that are the foundation of scientific computing, or have AI workloads just accelerated in time the path that scientific computing was already on? In this panel, our experts will examine this question, looking at the hardware and software that power the world’s largest supercomputers for both HPC and AI, and discuss the implications this has on organizations who rely on these systems and how this affects the next generation of professionals starting out in a supercomputing field that is changing faster than it has in its 60+ year history.

sess267.d:
Success in high performance computing (HPC) and research depends on bringing together diverse perspectives, experiences, and approaches to problem-solving. This panel explores the value of intergenerational collaboration in the workplace and how teams can thrive by leveraging the unique strengths of each generation.

Featuring professionals from a broad range of career stages, panelists will share their experiences working across generations, discuss common challenges and opportunities, and highlight strategies for building inclusive, high-performing teams. Attendees will gain insights into fostering mutual learning, bridging communication styles, and creating environments where institutional knowledge and fresh ideas come together to drive innovation.

Whether you are early in your career or a seasoned professional, this discussion will provide practical takeaways for strengthening collaboration and advancing success in the research and high performance computing community.

sess447.d: Bringing biomedical discoveries from the research environment to the bedside requires more than technology. It requires collaboration across disciplines, institutions, and perspectives. This panel brings together participants from the Regional Technical Hub representing academia, national laboratories, industry, and clinical practice to share their experiences using AI, high performance computing, and other advanced technologies to accelerate biomedical research and translation. Panelists will explore the opportunities and challenges of cross-disciplinary collaboration, translating innovation into practice, integrating new tools into clinical workflows, and responsibly working with sensitive biomedical and clinical data. Together, we will consider how we can bridge the translational gap and harness emerging technologies to improve outcomes for patients.

i: Northwestern Medicine Feinberg School of Medicine
University of Illinois Chicago College of Medicine

sess597.d: Elizabeth McNally, MD, PhD, is the Elizabeth J. Ward Professor of Genetic Medicine and director of the Center for Genetic Medicine. An international expert in the genetics of cardiovascular and neuromuscular disorders, McNally explores the genetic mechanisms responsible for inherited diseases such as heart failure, cardiomyopathy, muscular dystrophy and arrhythmias. Her laboratory establishes models for these disorders with the goal of developing novel therapeutic strategies such as gene editing. Her most recent work has investigated the effects of prednisone in reducing obesity in mice, uncovered new genetic variants linked to heart failure, and developed an antibody that could be used to treat muscular dystrophy. As director of the Center for Genetic Medicine, McNally leads the center in advancing scientific understanding of the genetic underpinnings of human disease and how to use this information to improve patient decision-making and therapies. McNally has earned widespread recognition for her contributions to science, including designation as a Distinguished Scientist by the American Heart Association, election to both the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the National Academy of Medicine, and receiving the American Heart Association Council on Genomics and Precision Medicine’s Medal of Honor. She has also served as president of the Association of American Physicians. In 2023, she was awarded the Martin E. and Gertrude G. Walder Award for Research Excellence. She currently serves as editor-in-chief of the Journal of Clinical Investigation.

sess602.d: Maria Jaromin brings a multidisciplinary background spanning computational engineering, technology transfer, research development, and compliance. She currently leads the Healthcare Innovation Program Office at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois Urbana‑Champaign. In this role, she fosters and advances cross‑disciplinary research collaborations across the university and with external partners, with a focus on integrating advanced technologies into health and biomedical research. Prior to her current position, Maria served as a Technology Manager in the Office of Technology Management at the University of Illinois System, where she managed an intellectual property portfolio in engineering and physical sciences. Her work included evaluating the patentability and commercialization potential of university innovations, negotiating legal agreements, and educating researchers on technology transfer processes and policies. Maria began her career at the Illinois Applied Research Institute as a Research Engineer, specializing in modeling and simulation to enhance the efficiency, safety, and performance of engineering systems and processes. She holds a bachelor’s and master’s degree in Power Engineering from the Silesian University of Technology in Gliwice, Poland; a Licentiate of Engineering in Energy Technology from the Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, Sweden; and an MBA from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

sess373.d: Testbeds play a vital role in assessing the readiness of novel architectures for upcoming supercomputers for the exascale and post-exascale era. These testbeds also act as co-design hubs, enabling the collection of application operational requirements, while identifying critical gaps that need to be addressed for an architecture to become viable for HPC. Various research centers are actively deploying testbeds, and our aim is to build a community that facilitates the sharing of information, encouraging collaboration and understanding of the available evaluation resources. This BoF will facilitate the exchange of best practices, including testbed design, benchmarking, system evaluation, and availability.

sess361.d: The rapid evolution of AI is driving unprecedented innovation in computing architectures, from GPUs and AI accelerators to novel memory, networking, and system designs. This BoF brings together leaders from industry, academia, and national laboratories to discuss emerging directions in AI acceleration for future zettascale systems. Rather than focusing on specific products, participants will explore common challenges in architecture, programmability, scalability, energy efficiency, software ecosystems, and deployment at scale. The session will emphasize audience interaction, community discussion, and roadmap development, providing attendees an opportunity to help shape the future of AI acceleration and AI-enabled supercomputing.

sess374.d: AI now drives discovery across HPC science, yet models are only as trustworthy as the data they use. Many teams still lack a shared way to judge whether their data is ready for AI. This BoF brings together the HPC and scientific communities to define data readiness for AI using seven practical dimensions: quality, understandability, fair and unbiased representation, structure and organization, feature importance, governance covering ethics, security and privacy, and AI-specific needs such as labels and distributions. Through short talks and open discussion, we will compare practices, identify gaps, and begin building shared metrics, tools, and benchmarks.

sess372.d: The implications of HPC technology on society and the environment prompt us, as a community, to discuss and understand our direct and indirect impacts. This BoF is highly interactive and aims to facilitate discussion within the community, relating ethical behavior and societal norms to the design of HPC solutions and autonomous/intelligent systems. The BoF will feature breakout groups and then converge to a plenum discussion. By furthering this dialogue, we can ensure that the HPC community advances its commitment to technology for the benefit of humanity as a whole. We do not expect to reach conclusions, but raise ideas.

i: French Institute for Research in Computer Science and Automation (INRIA)

sess369.d: Energy efficiency has evolved from an operational objective into a contractual engineering requirement for next-generation HPC systems. This BoF explores how procurement contracts shape future supercomputer design by comparing approaches from China, Japan, and Europe. Yutong Lu examines the architectural evolution from Tianhe-2A to CPU-based LineShine, highlighting CPU-based acceleration methods without relying on accelerator components. Masaaki Kondo presents Fugaku to FugakuNEXT, emphasizing procurement strategies for higher simulation performance within a power envelope. Maria Grazia Giuffreda discusses energy-to-solution requirements and software optimization clauses. An interactive forum debates how procurement clauses drive architectural choices, software portability, sustainability, and innovation in late-2020s deployments.

i: Erlangen National High Performance Computing Center
Energy Efficient High Performance Computing Working Group (EE HPC WG)
National Supercomputing Center in Guangzhou & Shenzhen

sess371.d: The “Julia for HPC” BoF provides a place for the HPC community with interests in the Julia programming language as an LLVM front-end to close the gaps between high-productivity languages and the performance of compiled languages. We invite participants from industry, government, and academia to discuss their experiences, identify and learn about opportunities and gaps. Topics include Julia adoption for quantum computing, auto-tuning, mixed precision, and agentic AI. The fifth consecutive BoF continues the “Julia for HPC” engagement with the SC community, and complements the tutorial on Julia for HPC at SC26. Presentations will be posted here: https://github.com/JuliaParallel/julia-hpc-bof-sc26.

i: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

sess362.d: What if we have been oversolving in computational science and engineering for decades? Are low-precision arithmetic formats only for AI workloads? How can HPC applications exploit mixed-precision hardware features? This BoF invites the HPC community at large interested in applying mixed precisions into their workflows and discussing the impact on time-to-solution, memory footprint, storage, data motion, and energy consumption. Experts from scientific applications/software libraries/hardware architectures will briefly provide the context on this trendy topic, share their own perspectives, and mostly engage with the audience via a set of questions, while gathering feedback to define a roadmap moving forward.

i: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Lincoln Laboratory

sess370.d: As demand for specialized architectures grows in the post-Moore era, this BoF will foster a sustained community around chip prototyping using open-source hardware tools. Building on themes explored in previous editions of this BoF at SC24 and SC25, the session will focus on practical tool experiences, current gaps, domain-specific accelerators, AI-assisted design workflows, and chip prototyping as an emerging HPC workload. Invited speakers from architecture, open-source EDA, accelerator design, and HPC will seed discussion. Expected outcomes include actionable insights, stronger collaboration, and follow-up community initiatives to advance open-source chip prototyping.

sess345.d: HPC centers are modernizing how they provision and operate clusters as systems become more heterogeneous, security-sensitive, and composable. OpenCHAMI, an HPSF emerging project, is an operator-led open-source control plane that brings cloud-like APIs and modular services to HPC system management. This BoF will help newcomers understand what OpenCHAMI enables today, give current users a forum to compare deployments and priorities, and invite operators, vendors, and developers to shape the roadmap. We will discuss adoption paths, including but not limited to xCAT transitions, and collect community feedback on tooling, integration, documentation, and operational requirements.

sess360.d: OpenSHMEM is a community-driven partitioned global address space (PGAS) API for low-overhead, one-sided asynchronous communication across diverse HPC architectures. This BoF will present progress since the 1.6 specification and discuss ongoing work toward OpenSHMEM 1.7, the proposed GPU auxiliary specification for accelerator support, and the longer-term OpenSHMEM 2.0 roadmap. As heterogeneous systems become the norm, the session will bring together users, implementers, middleware and tool developers, hardware vendors, and HPC facilities to share experiences, discuss evolving requirements, and help shape a simple, portable, and vendor-neutral future for OpenSHMEM.

sess364.d: Reproducibility remains a fundamental challenge for computational science and AI-enabled research. Building on successful BoFs at SC22, SC24, and PEARC22-PEARC25, we established the Reproducibility of Computational Research Community of Practice, which now includes an active mailing list, public website, webinar series, and emerging working groups. This interactive BoF will engage the SC26 community in shaping the next phase of this effort by sharing community progress, launching working groups, and exploring how AI can improve the capture of reproducible computational artifacts while addressing new challenges. The session welcomes researchers, research computing professionals, software developers, librarians, and cyberinfrastructure practitioners.

sess363.d: The SIGHPC Annual Member Meeting brings together ACM SIGHPC members and the broader HPC community to review the organization's activities, celebrate recent accomplishments, and discuss priorities for the coming year. The meeting provides an open forum where members can interact directly with SIGHPC leadership, learn about ongoing initiatives in education, awards, student programs, chapters, diversity and inclusion, publications, and conference activities, and help shape future directions. Whether you are a long-time member or new to the community, this session offers an opportunity to engage with SIGHPC leadership, provide feedback, ask questions, and become involved in the society's activities.

sess366.d: Python is the most widely used programming language today — but on HPC systems, it’s often more pain than power. From slow module loading on shared filesystems to packaging headaches and incompatible distributions, these hurdles block new users and frustrate seasoned developers alike. Meanwhile, major changes to Python’s core — new array APIs, packaging reforms, JIT compilation, and threading primitives — are happening without HPC at the table. This BoF brings together language leaders and HPC practitioners to shape Python’s future, learn what’s coming, and connect with peers.

sess368.d:
According to many mainstream media outlets and tech gurus, the age of computer programmers is fading away as GenAI proves itself capable of helping with programming tasks, or completing them independently. And many of us probably have positive (and negative) stories about using AI in our day-to-day lives. But what do we expect the impact of GenAI to be on programming for HPC systems and applications?

This session kicks off with opening statements from thought leaders representing various HPC programming models (MPI, OpenMP, NVIDIA, Kokkos, COMPSs, and Chapel), followed by an open session for audience opinions, Q&A, and healthy debate.

sess367.d: Originally GPU and CPU memory spaces were completely separate, with explicit data movements needed for interaction between CPU and GPU compute cores. Over time, all major GPU vendors have added hardware and software capabilities for transparent access to each other’s memory, with various levels of granularity and integration, with unified shared memory (USM) representing the most tight integration. This BoF will start by outlining the history, current state, and planned future of cross-memory technologies. We will then open the floor for discussion with conference attendees to gather their perspectives on where this technology should evolve going forward.

sess365.d:
This BoF will convene the workflows community to discuss the challenges of next-generation scientific workflows. A central focus will be on how the role of the human changes as workflows become increasingly autonomous: where people remain in the loop, how they steer and validate agentic systems, and how our community can support workflow developers.

The session will bring together workflow users, developers, theorists, and industrial collaborators, highlighting emerging research directions and practical needs from scientific campaigns. Through interactive discussions, participants will explore collaborative strategies to enable resilient, scalable, and adaptive workflows that meet the evolving demands of scientific discovery.

sess598.d: Robert L. Grossman, PhD, is the Frederick H. Rawson Distinguished Service Professor in Medicine and Computer Science and the Jim and Karen Frank Director of the Center for Translational Data Science at the University of Chicago. He joined the faculty in 2010 and served as the chief research informatics officer (CRIO) of the Biological Sciences Division from 2011-2024. He is also the Chief of the Section of Biomedical Data Science in the Department of Medicine. He is the principal investigator for the National Cancer Institute Genomic Data Commons (GDC), a platform for the cancer research community that manages, analyzes, integrates, and shares large-scale genomic datasets in support of precision medicine. The GDC is used by more than 150,000 researchers each month. He has also built data commons to support research in other areas, including cardiovascular diseases, infectious diseases and medical imaging. His research interests include data science, AI, and machine learning. He is the founder and a partner at Analytic Strategy Partners, which helps companies develop AI strategies, and a Director of the Open Commons Consortium (OCC), which is a not-for-profit that manages and operates data commons and data meshes to advance scientific and biomedical research. He served as a member of the NOAA Scientific Advisory Board (SAB) from 2017-2024 and as a member of the Frederick National Laboratory Advisory Committee (FNLAC) from 2014-2021. He earned his PhD in applied mathematics at Princeton University and an AB in mathematics from Harvard University.

sess465.d:
Designing and operating exascale infrastructure for HPC and AI workloads is no longer a distant challenge — it is accelerating faster than ever, bringing unprecedented complexity in performance, cost, scalability, and security. National labs, hyperscalers, neo-clouds, commercial enterprises, and academic centers all face these problems, often arriving at very different solutions shaped by their workloads, regulatory contexts, supply chains, and economics.

This 90-minute panel brings together operators from across the sector to compare approaches, debate trade-offs, and surface the practical lessons most worth carrying across organizational boundaries. Topics under discussion include cost-effective scaling, exascale data movement, security and multi-tenancy, energy and power management, and operational resilience.

The panel delivers insights that benefit the broader HPC and AI ecosystem — turning isolated operational lessons into a shared, comparative view, aligned with the theme of SC26: HPC Unites.

sess439.d:
Biomedical digital twins represent a frontier for exascale computing and AI, offering transformative potential for proactive healthcare, precision medicine, and medical-device innovation. However, translating complex human physiology into real-world clinical workflows introduces critical HPC challenges in model fidelity, speed, data integration, regulatory validation, and deployment cost.

This panel brings together leaders across academia, medical devices, and modeling software: Dr. Amanda Randles (Duke University; computational digital twins and HPC biophysical simulations), Darrell Swenson (Medtronic; HPC integration in medical device development), and Dr. Mark Palmer (Synopsys; clinical translation, simulation, and enterprise digital twin adoption). Using cardiac digital twins as a primary high-impact case study, the panel will explore the broader roadmap for biomedical HPC. The session is structured around interactive debate and direct audience engagement to address a central question: What must the supercomputing community solve next to make high-fidelity biological digital twins routine, scalable, and impactful across clinical and industrial settings?

sess599.d: Nicholas Chia is a Computational Biologist at Argonne National Laboratory whose work spans artificial intelligence, cancer biology, complex systems, and translational medicine. He received a B.S. in Physics from Georgetown University and a Ph.D. in Physics from The Ohio State University, followed by postdoctoral training in biocomplexity, collective effects, and evolution at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Prior to joining Argonne, Chia spent more than a decade at Mayo Clinic, where he served as Waterman Endowed Co-Chair of the Microbiome Program, Director of the Beyond DNA Multi-omics Strategic Theme within the Center for Individualized Medicine, Associate Director of the Microbiome Program, and Associate Professor of Medicine. During that time, he helped build Mayo’s microbiome and multiomics programs and contributed to the introduction of technologies that ultimately supported 19 laboratory-developed tests reaching clinical go-live. His research has focused on colorectal cancer, cancer evolution, microbial ecology, genome-scale metabolic modeling, and the integration of multi-omic data into clinical and biological discovery. He is recognized for early work applying inverse reinforcement learning to cancer evolution, framing tumor progression as an adaptive process and developing computational approaches to infer the evolutionary pressures that shape disease trajectories. At Argonne, his work has expanded into AI for Science, scientific reasoning, biological foundation models, and large-scale computational biology. He is a contributor to BioAlchemy, a large-scale biological reasoning corpus derived from the scientific literature, and leads and collaborates on programs spanning scientific reasoning, causal inference, disease modeling, population health, biological foundation models, and AI-enabled discovery. His work leverages leadership-class computing resources to develop and evaluate AI systems for scientific research. Across national laboratories, academic medicine, and interdisciplinary research programs, Chia has worked on problems that require the integration of large-scale data, mechanistic modeling, and decision-making under uncertainty, with applications ranging from cancer and microbiome science to scientific reasoning and AI-driven discovery.

sess600.d: Prem Kumar is the John A. Dever Professor of Information Technology at the McCormick School of Engineering and Applied Science at Northwestern University. His primary research focus is on photonic devices and their applications utilizing the principles of nonlinear and quantum optics (>$30M cumulative research funding). Recent projects have included: generation, distribution, and ultrafast processing of photonic entanglement for applications in quantum information networks; novel quantum light states for precision measurements, imaging, and sensing; and novel optical amplifiers and devices for networked classical optical communications. Although Dr. Kumar’s primary appointment is in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, an affiliation with the Applied Physics program allows him to recruit multidisciplinary students into his research group, a privilege that has proven extremely beneficial for his research interests that lie at the interface of basic quantum science and applied information technology. Because of this interdisciplinary exposure, Ph.D. graduates from his research group (37 completed, 5 in progress) have gone on to build careers in academia, industry, and US national labs. His group has cumulatively published >500 research papers (Google Scholar h-index: 69), including 1 edited book, 2 book chapters, 6 patents, >200 peer-reviewed journal papers, 45 articles in hard-bound volumes, and >300 conference papers with >100 invited. From Feb’13 to Jan’17, Dr. Kumar was on leave from Northwestern to be at DARPA, where he served as a Program Manager in the Defense Sciences Office. At DARPA, Dr. Kumar created and managed a ~$20M/year portfolio of programs in basic and applied sciences, targeting a diverse range of topics that included neuroscience and engineering, ultrafast laser science and technology, precision navigation and timing, stand-off chem-bio defense, quantum effects in biological environments, and quantum information science and technology. He was also program manager for the Defense Science Study Group, which allowed him to interact with young academic faculty from universities across the US in various national defense settings. For his strong portfolio of programs in basic science and technology and his mentoring of DARPA Risers—young, noteworthy performers on DARPA programs—Dr. Kumar was selected Program Manager of the Year in 2015 and awarded the Secretary of Defense Medal for Outstanding Public Service in 2016. Prior to joining DARPA, Dr. Kumar served on the National Academies Committee that issued the 2012 landmark study: “Optics and Photonics: Essential Technologies for Our Nation,” which spawned the National Photonics Initiative (NPI). From 2018 to 2024, Dr. Kumar served on the NPI Steering Committee, lending his expertise to issues pertaining to the National Quantum Initiative. Dr. Kumar is a Fellow of Optica (formerly OSA), APS, IEEE, IoP (U.K.), AAAS, and SPIE. He has been a Distinguished Lecturer for the IEEE Photonics Society, Hermann A. Haus Lecturer at MIT, recipient of the Quantum Communication Award from Tamagawa University in Tokyo, Japan, and the Walder Research Excellence Award from the Provost’s office at Northwestern University. From 2020 to 2025, he served as the Editor-in-Chief of Optica, the flagship journal of The Optica Publishing Group (formerly OSA) for high-impact research. Currently, he co-chairs the National Academies Committee on Atomic Molecular and Optical Sciences, and was recently appointed to the External Advisory Board for NTT Basic Research Laboratories in Atsugi, Japan. Internal to Northwestern, he serves on the Executive Committee for the Institute at Northwestern for Quantum Information Research and Engineering (INQUIRE). Beginning Fall’26, he will also serve as the Interim Chair of the Electrical and Computer Engineering Department.

sess255.d: The first CUDA-capable GPU was launched 20 years ago, and a sparse matrix-vector product (SpMV) kernel was one of the first CUDA kernels I attempted to write. The SIMT execution model of the GPU made it relatively easy to build a working implementation, but the simplest kernels suffered from several performance pitfalls. A couple of years later, Nathan Bell and I set out to design kernels that would deliver truly high throughput and utilize significant fractions of the high bandwidth that GPUs provide. The paper we published in SC09 demonstrated that this was indeed possible. It also highlighted two key ideas: selecting the right data structure that exploits known matrix structure makes high performance straightforward, and irregularity is easily managed if it is rare. Since that time, a great deal of work has been done for both sparse computations and linear algebra on the GPU. In this talk, I will look back at the lessons of our early work, some notable steps on the path since that time, and consider some of the challenges ahead of us.

sess448.d: A decade ago, in 2016, the U.S. National Cancer Institute and the U.S. Department of Energy announced their truly unique collaboration to take advantage of each agency's strengths, bringing together the power of emerging exascale systems and the collective data, knowledge, and wisdom of the cancer community. With the advances of the last decade in HPC, AI, and availability of cancer clinical and research data, the opportunities ahead are tremendous to improve cancer care. Enabled by HPC, the next decade will be truly transformative as clinical opportunities and potential are realized, research connections are made, and the paths for translation of data science insights to treat patients are widened. The panel will reflect on the experiences and advances of the past decade, share insights on current challenges, and look ahead to the future as HPC unites communities to take on cancer.

i: Frederick National Laboratory for Cancer Research

sess467.d: The explosive scale of generative AI models demands highly specialized infrastructure. This panel explores the critical challenges of building and scaling dedicated AI clusters tailored specifically to the modern model lifecycle: massive-scale pre-training, nuanced post-training, and high-throughput, capacity-demanding inference. As models scale to trillions of parameters, infrastructure must deliver unprecedented compute density, ultra-low latency interconnects, data processing, reliability requirements, parallelisms, and continuous I/O throughput. Our panelists will dissect the unique hardware and software bottlenecks inherent to each phase. We will debate the most effective strategies for mitigating hardware failures at scale, optimizing distributed storage pipelines, and tackling power constraints. This interactive 90-minute session will equip attendees with actionable insights into architecting the resilient, high-performance systems required to power the next generation of generative AI breakthroughs.

sess604.d: John Towns is the Deputy Director at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications. He leads the NSF-funded ACCESS Coordination Office, as part of the overall ACCESS Program supporting researchers and educators nation-wide in the use of advanced computing systems, and plays key roles in the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) Pilot as co-Chair of the Allocations Working Group and Chair of the Coordination Team. He also serves as executive sponsor of NCSA’s Quantum Program Office, a partnership with the Illinois Quantum Information Science and Technology Center (IQUIST), to advance quantum research. With over 35 years of experience, Towns has held leadership roles in numerous national and international initiatives supporting advanced research computing. He holds M.S. degrees in Physics and Astronomy from the University of Illinois and a B.S. in Physics from the University of Missouri-Rolla.

sess601.d: Volodymyr Kindratenko serves as the Assistant Director at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he also holds the position of Director for the Center for Artificial Intelligence Innovation (CAII). He is an Adjunct Associate Professor in the Departments of Electrical and Computer Engineering and a Research Associate Professor in the Siebel School of Computing and Data Science. Prior to his current role, Dr. Kindratenko led NCSA's Innovative Systems Laboratory, a center-wide research initiative focused on evaluating emerging computing technologies for high-performance computing applications. Dr. Kindratenko earned his D.Sc. degree from the University of Antwerp, Belgium, in 1997. His research interests encompass high-performance computing, special-purpose computing architectures, cloud computing, and machine learning systems and applications. His work has received funding from NSF, NASA, ONR, DOE, and industry. Dr. Kindratenko has published over 140 papers in refereed scientific journals and conference proceedings and holds five US patents.

sess381.d: AI applications increasingly span a computing continuum from edge sensors through cloud to HPC centers, yet most are still assembled and operated manually. This BoF convenes the SC community around agentic, service-oriented cyberinfrastructure: software agents, exposed as composable services, that sense continuum state, decide where to train and deploy models, act through a shared control plane, and learn from outcomes. Drawing on experience from the NSF ICICLE AI Institute and invited external perspectives, participants will debate autonomy levels, trust, provenance, evaluation, and emerging protocols such as MCP, and identify steps toward community benchmarks and interoperable agentic cyberinfrastructure.

sess375.d: Building on a decade of Americas HPC Collaboration (AHPC) BoFs, this SC26 session will formalize the Education and Workforce Development Chapter and outline a practical roadmap for its first year. The BoF will focus on areas where collaboration can make a concrete impact: system-facing training for people who deploy and support HPC/AI infrastructure, using the Oak Ridge Computing Academy (ORCA) as one example; a panel on emerging AI and quantum training needs with academia and industry participants; and student cluster competition experiences that demonstrate the value of hands-on learning. Participants will identify shared assets, pilot activities, and institutional commitments.

i: National Laboratory of Scientific Computing (LNCC), Brazil

sess382.d: As HPC accelerates into an era of hybrid infrastructure and pervasive AI, computational research increasingly calls for optimizing blended on-prem and cloud infrastructure for advanced workflows that will accelerate future discoveries. This session begins with the drivers: cutting-edge science workflows challenging traditional infrastructure, and agentic AI workflows that autonomously drive the entire scientific loop from hypothesis generation to results analysis. We then review the current capabilities and gaps for managing and using blended HPC infrastructure as the backbone of these advanced workflows. Attendees will engage in discussion and interactive polling, collaboratively identifying gaps and opportunities for the community to address.

sess414.d: Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific discovery, but today's cyberinfrastructure was designed for workflows in which data are collected, stored, analyzed, and archived as largely independent activities. Modern science increasingly requires continuous interaction among instruments, data repositories, workflows, AI services, edge devices, HPC systems, and scientists across institutional boundaries. This BoF brings together researchers, facility operators, cyberinfrastructure developers, and domain scientists to discuss the next generation of scientific data infrastructure. Through examples from astronomy, geosciences, materials science, medicine, and high-energy physics, participants will identify common infrastructure challenges and define a community roadmap for interoperable, federated scientific data ecosystems.

sess380.d: Sensitive workloads across health sciences, financial modeling, and AI/ML on proprietary data increasingly demand confidentiality guarantees traditionally out of scope for supercomputing infrastructure. Confidential computing—hardware-enforced trusted execution environments established in cloud and edge contexts—is proposed as a path to securing computation at HPC scale. But is this achievable, or does it conflict with the principles that make supercomputers fast? This BoF gathers the HPC community to debate whether confidential supercomputing is a necessary, achievable evolution or an aspirational posture satisfying compliance optics without meaningful security. Join us to map where it genuinely delivers—and where gaps remain.

sess403.d: The HPC community now has a working definition of the digital twin, anchored in the 2024 NASEM report. What it lacks are standards to operationalize that definition across the full lifecycle. This BoF brings together practitioners from novice to expert, spanning scientific computing, biomedicine, infrastructure, and data centers, to surface the most urgent gaps: data homogenization across heterogeneous sources, verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ) at every lifecycle stage, and the emerging role of agentic AI as both enabler and new source of complexity. We will map the landscape, identify active efforts, and determine what coordinated community action looks like.

sess379.d: AI is rapidly reshaping scientific software through code generation, simulation acceleration, intelligent workflows, and emerging agentic systems. Yet the software ecosystems, collaboration models, trust frameworks, and workforce practices that underpin high performance computing (HPC) were built for a different era. Drawing on findings from a recent workshop series (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03413), this BoF invites the international community to challenge assumptions, identify emerging priorities, and help define the next generation of scientific computing ecosystems. Discussion will focus on human-AI collaboration, trust, sustainability, user experience, and workforce evolution — turning shared insights into actionable directions for the community.

i: French Institute for Research in Computer Science and Automation (INRIA)

sess383.d:
The HPC Carpentry project, an effort to provide hands-on workshop-based instruction for novice users of HPC systems, has long been well-aligned with the broader educational mission of the Carpentries project, using open-source materials to bridge the gap between resources and the skills needed to use them effectively.

Having been adopted as a new lesson program within the Carpentries, it is time to reconnect with the larger HPC community, seeking feedback on strategic planning, and identifying new audiences where the solutions developed during the Carpentries incubation and adoption process can add value and strengthen the world of HPC education.

i: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

sess384.d: Graph analytics is foundational to scientific discovery, national security, artificial intelligence (AI), and industrial innovation, yet sparse, irregular, and evolving graph workloads continue to challenge HPC systems. This BoF convenes developers and users of high-performance graph toolkits to exchange updates, compare combinatorial and algebraic approaches, and define priorities for converged workflows spanning simulation, data analytics, AI, instruments, edge platforms, clouds, and supercomputers. Discussion will address GraphBLAS, interoperability, dynamic graphs, heterogeneous execution, provenance, trustworthy reasoning, and sustainable open infrastructure, producing concrete community directions for research, software, standards, benchmarks, infrastructure investment, and cross-sector collaboration. The outcome will guide collaborative work beyond SC26.

i: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center

sess377.d: As direct liquid cooling scales, the interface between IT systems and facility mechanical infrastructure becomes more critical. This BoF explores four challenges. First, high-temperature cooling (heat-reuse, IT thermal margins) and dew point (prevent condensation). Second, warm-water fluid quality (filtration and added chemicals to prevent corrosion, biological growth, and scaling). Third, temperature and fluid dynamics with rapid workload power swings (volumetric expansion, pump cavitation, facility response characteristics). Fourth, integrating telemetry into IT systems and building automation (predict thermal excursions, reduce trapped capacity). This session is intended for facility engineers, system integrators, operations, administrators, architects, and researchers in energy-efficiency and sustainability.

i: Energy Efficient High Performance Computing Working Group (EE HPC WG)
Energy Efficient High Performance Computing Working Group (EE HPC WG)

sess386.d: Through its mission to reduce time to science by nurturing parallel computing skills, the Open Accelerated Computing Consortium (OpenACC) invites you to explore the future of directive-based programming. In the age of agentic coding assistants, this BoF examines the evolving roles of OpenACC, OpenMP, standard language parallelism, and abstraction libraries like Julia for Accelerators or Kokkos for GPU-resident runtimes. Panels including compiler developers and community leaders will summarize the current state of programming for accelerators, followed by open discussion comparing practices and imagining new futures. Developers, researchers, compiler vendors, and the broader HPC community are welcome to shape the conversation.

i: NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR)

sess349.d:
The TOP500 list of supercomputers serves as a “Who’s Who” in the field of high performance computing (HPC). It started as a list of the most powerful supercomputers in the world and has evolved to a major source of information about trends in HPC. The 68th TOP500 list will be published in November 2026, just in time for SC26.

This BoF will present detailed analyses of the TOP500 and discuss the changes in the HPC marketplace during the past years. The BoF is meant as an open forum for discussion and feedback between the TOP500 authors and the user community.

sess378.d: Federated learning (FL) lets institutions train shared AI models without exchanging raw data — a capability increasingly essential for science where data is sensitive, proprietary, or too large to move. Yet FL on HPC remains uncharted: job schedulers, site firewalls, identity federation, and heterogeneous accelerators reshape the problem beyond what cloud-based FL assumes. This BoF brings together framework developers, HPC centers, and scientific users to discuss running trustworthy FL across the world's supercomputers. We will surface open algorithmic, systems, and governance challenges and work toward a community roadmap for cross-facility FL benchmarks, interoperability, and shared practice.

sess346.d: The U.S. National Science Foundation asked the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to assess the evolving role of cyberinfrastructure in enabling 21st-century scientific discovery and innovation. This Birds of a Feather session will discuss the committee’s assessment of NSF’s advanced cyberinfrastructure portfolio in a rapidly changing environment shaped by artificial intelligence, cloud computing, rapidly expanding private-sector investment in AI, and the potential role of strategic partnership between government and industry. Committee members will summarize major themes from the report and invite community discussion on how NSF can sustain broad, effective, and forward-looking cyberinfrastructure for the research enterprise.

i: National Academies of Engineering, Science, and Medicine

sess387.d: HPC systems were built for trusted users. Today they run a variety of HPC and AI workloads, serve GPU-as-a-service customers they've never met, and face rising regulatory attention. NIST is finalizing SP 800-234, the first HPC-specific security overlay, and advanced compute is one of the few genuinely bipartisan topics in Washington. The rules are coming. The question is whether operators shape them or inherit them. This BoF brings standards authors, security architects, supercomputing operators, and implementers into a candid, practitioner-level exchange with the audience on what works, what fails, and how the community secures shared compute without slowing the science.

i: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
Erlangen National High Performance Computing Center

Using your registration details, we’ll generate a one-of-a-kind fractal image just for you — sent to you and showcased on displays throughout the conference. Creativity has always been at the heart of innovation. It drives new perspectives, fuels artistic expression, and allows us to see beauty in unexpected places.
