sess240.d: SCC Connect is a companion to the Student Cluster Competition (SCC) with a focus on accessibility and education. Using provided, cloud-based hardware, SCC Connect teams build and run benchmarks and a selection of real HPC workloads in a two-day nonstop competition. Teams compete remotely from all around the world, and several teams will attend SC26 and compete from booths in the Exhibit Hall. Come by to meet the teams and cheer them on!

sess449.d:
The AI and HPC community is scrambling to accommodate the explosive demand for memory and storage capacity and new technologies. Does one solution fit all in storage components and architectures? What new differentiators matter across varied usages like out-of-core HPC computation on huge data sets, context memory cache capacity for LLM inference, 10x-higher IOPs for vector databases and GNNs, scaled checkpointing, and multitenant security?

To spark creativity and frame emerging opportunities, this panel gathers leading experts from academia in usage models, and vendor technologists for storage microcontrollers, object/file systems, and network storage acceleration that engage in storage innovation. The audience will gain new knowledge of emerging tech and new perspectives on topics that they may have recently heard of. Just as for each of the last several years of this Panel/BoF, speakers and audience contributors will archive reference material to accelerate moving the broader community forward.
Panel Session Link

sess462.d: Medical digital twins are an exciting area of investment and rapid innovation and hold tremendous potential to realize the promise of precision medicine and improved health. The successful adoption of medical digital twin approaches requires a community effort, spanning a full range of stakeholders with the individual or patient at the center. With an esteemed group of experts in medical digital twins, the panel will help attendees understand the world of medical digital twins, what it means and what it holds in store. The panel will also discuss several areas where HPC plays or could play a role in helping to unify and connect medical digital twin stakeholders in such areas as varying disciplines, anatomical systems, interoperability, data access and privacy, proprietary and open, AI and mechanistic models, clinics and research, education, and many more areas essential to the development and adoption of medical digital twins.

i: University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center

sess398.d: Providing simplified access to distributed HPC, AI, and cloud resources is a global challenge. Driven by major investments and user demand for a single pane of glass, the need for interoperable resource portals is clear—yet implementations that work across institutional and national boundaries remain hard. Following a well-received ISC 2026 BoF, this session broadens the conversation to operators of federated research infrastructures across Europe, the U.S., and Asia-Pacific, sharing experiences, challenges overcome, and lessons learned. Through lightning updates, live polling, and moderated discussion, attendees exchange practical approaches to federated identity, allocation, accounting, and site autonomy versus federated consistency.

sess388.d: Fortran plays a crucial role in numerous applications. This BoF provides a forum for Fortran developers to engage with the language's modern programming features. With features introduced in recent language revisions, Fortran 2023 supports modern programming practices and high performance computing (HPC). This BoF gathers developers from diverse domains to share experiences and explore Fortran's evolving capabilities. After some brief presentations, the session will focus on an interactive discussion where audience members will be encouraged to share their own experiences and ask questions of our experts.

sess394.d: Autonomous experiment operation is demonstrating the ability to dramatically improve the pace of scientific discovery. This BoF convenes a community to continue building on the early two-year roadmap, discussing how different teams are using agentic workflows to improve the potential for new discovery and to address the related need to verify the new results.

sess390.d: The world's largest supercomputers for scientific discovery are also premier systems for artificial intelligence model training and inference. While traditional HPC compute has predominately leveraged the MPI standard, AI workloads have increasingly focused on collective communication libraries, such as NVIDIA's NCCL and AMD's RCCL, which are optimized for high throughput and GPU-native usage. This Birds of a Feather (BoF) session at the SC Conference (SC) aims to delve into the intricacies of collective communication libraries, focusing on the comparison between the widely adopted Message Passing Interface (MPI) and NCCL/RCCL, as well as other key messaging libraries, such as SHMEM.

sess389.d: Effective software testing plays a critical role in guaranteeing the performance, correctness, and reproducibility of software. Testing high-performance computing (HPC) software poses unique challenges due to massive parallelism, concurrency and heterogeneity, the scale of target platforms, lack of oracles, and application-specific verification and verification. These challenges are now amplified by AI coding tools generating and translating HPC code faster than humans can review it. In this BoF, a panel of experts and the audience will discuss methodologies and challenges in HPC software testing, including verification of AI-generated code to deepen our understanding of this crucial aspect of HPC software development.

sess392.d: The growing interest in fusion energy to power massive data centers has created an urgent need to accelerate plasma science codes. Both experimental capabilities and computational workflows are complex and often render current technologies inefficient, which results in a severe lack of data. Implementation of plasma codes becomes complicated due to variations in software and hardware architectures. A potential solution is to develop an abstraction layer to connect infrastructure to application codes. This BoF focuses on identifying the needs for development and standardization of an abstraction layer, and the relevant functionalities/data structures that would be most useful to abstract.

sess426.d: In the near future (if not already) HPC software will be generated by AI. The question is not “if” we must adapt, but “how” we will adapt. Everything about our software will be impacted. In this BoF, we will focus on training: How does what we teach have to change to accommodate the necessary shift in skills in the AI era? We need ideas from across the community and people who will dedicate the time to debate these ideas, digest them, and produce a position paper to drive the change we need in HPC. It all starts with this BoF.

i: EPCC at the University of Edinburgh

sess396.d: The IO500 is the de facto benchmark standard for HPC storage. Official IO500 lists have been released at ISC and SC events since SC17 and now have over 300 entries. The purpose is to foster the high-performance storage community and ensure forward progress towards the common goals of creating, sharing, and benefiting from a large corpus of shared storage data. IO500 also serves as the largest repository of detailed HPC storage information for researchers and system designers to analyze and evaluate over time. A key BoF highlight is the presentation of the latest IO500 Production and Research lists.

sess397.d: With the increasing demand for AI in HPC, there has been a rapid rise in accelerated architectures, portable programming models, and frameworks. The already-daunting task of programming for interconnected accelerated systems has become even more complex. This BoF, organized by IXPUG, will focus on portable programming across a wide range of heterogeneous architectures—including Intel, NVIDIA, AMD, and ARM supporting diverse simulation, data analytics, and AI workloads. The session will explore key challenges, state-of-the-art solutions, and emerging best practices for programming across these systems, identifying common principles and methodologies that support development and long-term maintenance across sites, architectures, and scientific applications.

i: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

sess393.d: The Message Passing Interface (MPI) API is the most dominant programming approach for HPC environments. Its specification is driven by the MPI Forum, an open forum consisting of MPI developers, vendors, and users. This year, the MPI Forum published the latest version of the standard, MPI 5.0. We will take a look at the new features and will discuss what they mean for the users of MPI. We will also discuss ongoing work toward the next version of the MPI standard, with lightning talks from the working groups, and get feedback from the community.

sess391.d: This BoF is meant to be an open discussion to guide the future roadmap for Open OnDemand (openondemand.org), by getting feedback from the community on the prioritization of the various tasks planned for the next few years. OOD is extremely relevant to ongoing discussions within the HPC community about user interfaces and science gateways. The session leaders, all part of the OOD development team, will jointly develop the content for the presentation in advance to ensure a wide range of viewpoints and topics are presented. We will also consult with our user advisory group in advance for their suggestions.

sess402.d: Quantum computing resources are increasingly integrated into HPC and cloud environments, but software stacks remain isolated, vendor-specific, and often proprietary. OpenQSE is a community effort developing an open, modular ecosystem of vendor-neutral specifications to close the interoperability gaps that fragment hybrid quantum-classical workflows. This BoF will briefly share the initiative's roadmap and working-group progress, then open the floor for structured discussion with HPC facility staff, application teams, vendors, and researchers to identify priorities and shape the direction together. The intended outcome is a prioritized set of integration artifacts the community identifies as most urgent for near-term development.

sess395.d: Operational data analytics (ODA) has become essential for understanding and optimizing HPC systems. However, converting the vast amounts of operational data they generate into actionable insights still requires significant manual effort and domain expertise. Agentic AI has the potential to extend traditional analytics by reading telemetry, correlating signals, diagnosing problems, and drafting fixes for an operator to approve. This BoF will explore the state of the art in agentic AI’s applicability to ODA, promising use cases, limitations, and governance challenges. Participants will share experiences and discuss how agentic AI can enhance future HPC operations and efficiency.

i: Energy Efficient High Performance Computing Working Group (EE HPC WG)

sess347.d: As AI and HPC systems scale to unprecedented levels, traditional electrical interconnects are becoming a limiting factor. Silicon photonics offers a promising path to address bandwidth, energy efficiency and interconnect scalability constraints, but questions remain around deployment readiness, integration complexity and ecosystem maturity. Led by industry analyst Dan Olds, this session brings together experts from Penguin Solutions, Marvell and Micron to explore photonic interconnects from multiple perspectives. Panelists will discuss the technology’s value today, the technical and operational challenges ahead, where photonics can make the greatest impact, and what the broader ecosystem must do to accelerate real-world adoption.

sess401.d: User experience (UX) is often misunderstood as a nice-to-have, rather than a necessary element of scientific computing. In reality, UX encompasses all the ways a user interacts with a product and is highly relevant to HPC systems. This interactive BoF will introduce UX work as a practical approach for improving usability and adoption. Participants will discuss how to ask users better questions to uncover needs and identify opportunities to improve systems, services, and support. Participants will leave with practical methods, starter resources, and connections to a growing cross-institutional UX community. This session benefits developers, documentation specialists, and facility support staff.

sess400.d:
In order to exploit the capabilities of new HPC systems and to meet their demands in scalability, communication software needs to scale to millions of cores and support applications with adequate functionality. UCX is a collaboration between industry, national labs, and academia that consolidates and provides a unified open-source framework.

The UCX project is managed by the UCF Consortium (http://www.ucfconsortium.org/). The session will serve as the UCX community meeting and will introduce the latest developments to HPC developers and the broader user community.

sess450.d: This session examines how state and regional initiatives can strengthen U.S. leadership in AI and quantum computing. Using Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Utah, Oklahoma, and others as examples, the panel will explore how states are aligning regional assets with America’s AI Action Plan, the Genesis Mission, and the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR). The discussion frames this work as a grassroots U.S. counterpart to the EU “AI Continent,” built through state-led, place-based innovation rather than a top-down model. Building on the NSF-CASC Workshop on Envisioning NAIRR State and Regional Hubs for Educational Transformation, the session will highlight pathways for expanding workforce development, research access, and regional cooperation. Panelists will discuss partnerships among academia, government, industry, philanthropy, and federal agencies, along with strategies for broadening access to computing and data resources, streamlining deployment, and engaging states in AI capacity building. Inclusive state-led hubs can drive innovation, attract investment, and grow the AI workforce.

sess268.d: Active-duty servicemen and veterans are part of the workforce in high performance computing (HPC). This panel features speakers with a broad range of experience in HPC who will discuss strategies and leveraging training and skills, and how it translates into working in industry, academia and national laboratories.

sess463.d:
As memory-bound workloads begin to dominate HPC and AI, traditional architectures face severe limitations in memory bandwidth and capacity. Compute Express Link® (CXL®) is providing the means to create disaggregated and composable memory tiers to accelerate HPC and AI performance.

This panel, moderated by Dan Olds, features experts from Penguin Solutions, SemiconDx, and Intel, who will explore the evolving role of CXL in next-generation HPC/AI systems. Panelists will discuss emerging memory architectures, performance benchmarks, cost and scale trade-offs, alongside lessons learned from early implementations and incorporation of emerging technologies, such as silicon photonics, that should be on everyone’s roadmap.

Through interactive discussion and audience engagement, the session will highlight real-world benchmarks discussing CXL-enabled systems, as well as practical insights into memory-constrained workloads. Attendees will understand current limitations, gain actionable guidance, and leave better equipped to evaluate and resolve memory constraints in HPC and AI environments.

sess610.d:
Michelle Hoffmann, Ph.D. has been serving since August of 2021 as the Executive Director of the Chicago Biomedical Consortium (CBC), a consortium of biomedical researchers across Northwestern, the University of Illinois at Chicago, the University of Chicago, and six other Chicagoland institutions, that is generously supported by the Searle Funds at The Chicago Community Trust (CCT), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and The Walder Foundation. The CBC's mission is to find and fund research that will most likely become commercial biomedical applications driving Illinois's economic development.

In her time as Executive Director, Dr. Hoffmann has reorganized the CBC, developed a process to scout and build biopharma applications of Illinois's academic researchers, organized the greater entrepreneurial community and market it to coastal investors and biotech, and trained local PhD talent in the business of early science commercialization. Before this role, from 2019-2021, Dr. Hoffmann was the Senior Vice President of Deep Tech at P33, a privately funded nonprofit charged with elevating Chicagoland's innovation economy and driving inclusive economic growth.

Before P33, Hoffmann spent 15 years helping life sciences companies grow, most recently as a senior vice president at Boston-based Back Bay Life Science Advisors, an integrated strategy and investment firm for global life science companies, venture-backed startups and their investors. During her nine years at Back Bay, Hoffmann led projects for large, publicly traded companies and small, private, venture-backed health care and life sciences companies.

sess464.d: High performance computing is rapidly integrating machine learning with traditional numerical solvers, creating hybrid workflows and digital twins. This panel audits the "total energy to solution" for hybrid HPC workloads, quantifying their operational power demands from silicon hardware to total cost of ownership. Panelists will address the following core questions: What is the energy required to generate large-scale, ground-truth training datasets versus the direct computational cost of ML training? What, if any, is the energy overhead of running traditional physics engines alongside ML for active validation? At what computational breakeven point does deploying an ML surrogate yield a net reduction in total energy use? Finally, how do these physical energy ledgers translate into real-world budgets and sustainability goals for scientific deployment? Bringing together perspectives from materials science, weather forecasting, hyperscale computing, and computing economics, this panel evaluates the physical and financial energy realities of ML integration in HPC.

sess451.d:
High performance computing (HPC) is undergoing rapid transformation with the convergence of simulation, AI, data-intensive science, and emerging quantum computing. This evolution is reshaping the skills required to effectively use and advance these systems, creating urgent challenges in workforce development. This panel brings together perspectives from national laboratories, academia, and industry to discuss how to build a sustainable, inclusive, and future-ready HPC workforce.

Key questions include: What will the HPC workforce need to look like in the next 5–10 years? Where are the most critical gaps in skills, training pathways, and access? What skills are currently missing or undervalued in existing curricula? Which collaboration models across institutions have proven effective? How can we broaden participation and lower barriers to entry?

The session will include interactive audience engagement, with opportunities to submit and prioritize questions in real time, ensuring a dynamic and relevant discussion.

i: National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC)

sess612.d: Volodymyr Kindratenko serves as the Assistant Director at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he also holds the position of Director for the Center for Artificial Intelligence Innovation (CAII). He is an Adjunct Associate Professor in the Departments of Electrical and Computer Engineering and a Research Associate Professor in the Siebel School of Computing and Data Science. Prior to his current role, Dr. Kindratenko led NCSA's Innovative Systems Laboratory, a center-wide research initiative focused on evaluating emerging computing technologies for high-performance computing applications. Dr. Kindratenko earned his D.Sc. degree from the University of Antwerp, Belgium, in 1997. His research interests encompass high-performance computing, special-purpose computing architectures, cloud computing, and machine learning systems and applications. His work has received funding from NSF, NASA, ONR, DOE, and industry. Dr. Kindratenko has published over 140 papers in refereed scientific journals and conference proceedings and holds five US patents.

sess258.d:
Join us at McCormick Place in the South Lobby of the Grand Ballroom for the SC Students and Alumni Reception, an evening of HPC, machine learning, and quantum computing mysteries. Compare theories, trade debugging stories, and meet someone new.

Participants will have the opportunity to meet each other and VIP guests, hear about their career paths, and ask questions or exchange advice one-on-one. Throughout the evening, we will solve riddles inspired by the real pitfalls of advanced computing. Hors d’oeuvres will be served, and SC swag raffles will take place at 5:00, 5:30, and 6:00 p.m. We want to bring together all registered students, Early Career Program participants, alumni, and VIPs to create as many opportunities for networking and engagement as possible.

Here is your first mystery:

The case of the simulation that refused to finish

A simulation must count twenty million events before it stops. On the workstation, it finishes. On the accelerator, it runs indefinitely. The accelerator is still processing events. No error is reported. Its counter has reached 16,777,216 and will not move, although the program keeps adding one.

What has the machine run out of?

Come prepared to solve more mysteries and make connections.

sess406.d: HPC facilities each build operational data analytics in isolation, with no shared benchmarks to compare methods or reproduce results across sites. This seventh-edition BoF convenes the community around a common goal: shared standards, open benchmarks, and cross-facility collaboration for HPC workload analysis. Using the HPC ODA Commons, introduced to the community at ISC 2026, as a working exemplar, we examine how standardized schemas and benchmark recipes enable reproducible comparison across systems. We present an emerging multi-facility study, invite sites to contribute data, schemas, or models, and work together to prioritize analyses and plan a community report.

sess405.d: Analog computing is re-emerging as a broad approach to scientific computation, offering opportunities beyond energy efficiency, including low-latency physical dynamics, reduced data movement, computation integrated with sensing, and new methods for simulation, optimization, and artificial intelligence. Yet progress remains fragmented across physical substrates, applications, architectures, mathematics, and software. This highly interactive BoF will bring the SC community together to identify challenges, promising workloads, shared infrastructure, and opportunities for collaboration. Building on the DOE ASCR report Basic Research Needs for Analog Computing for Science, participants will prioritize research directions and help shape a community agenda for analog and hybrid analog-digital computing.

sess415.d: As AI rapidly reshapes public interest in computing, the HPC community has a unique opportunity to demystify these technologies and introduce foundational computational concepts. This interactive Birds of a Feather (BoF) session brings together HPC educators, trainers, and outreach practitioners to explore, facilitate, and evaluate hands-on AI outreach activities. Participants will test proven activities, discuss engagement best practices, and collaborate to design new resources using both human-led and AI-assisted frameworks. Attendees will walk away with a toolkit of reusable activities, insights into AI-driven content generation, and a collaborative network to strengthen HPC outreach community-wide.

i: Statewide California Earthquake Center, University of Southern California

sess407.d: Initiated at SC25 to explore AI inference services in the academic HPC community, this BoF returns to address the fast-evolving landscape of inference services, agentic AI, tool services, and AI4Science. This practitioner forum brings centers and researchers together to share practical insights and experiences spanning infrastructure, software, and use cases. This session aims to cultivate collaborative solutions for AI developments. The goal remains to foster a sustained, cross-institutional "community of practice" bridging academic and governmental HPC centers and the user community to foster collaborations in this area.

i: The University of Texas at Austin
National Center for High-Performance Computing (NCHC), Taiwan
National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science & Technology
NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR)

sess412.d: The OpenMP Architecture Review Board releases new versions of OpenMP every 2-3 years. This year, we will release OpenMP API version 6.1 just before SC26. Feature champions from the OpenMP Language committee will highlight key features in the OpenMP API version 6.1 through short lightning talks with rounds of discussion to give participants ample opportunity to interact with OpenMP experts, ask questions, and provide feedback. We will also include talks from vendors supporting compilers to discuss timelines for support of OpenMP API features.

sess404.d: As AI workloads scale exponentially, evaluating machine learning infrastructure requires rigorous, standardized benchmarking. This Birds of a Feather session brings together HPC researchers, hardware architects, and software engineers to discuss the future of the MLPerf benchmark suite. The discussion will address critical scaling challenges, heterogeneous accelerator evaluation, and performance metrics for disaggregated infrastructure. Participants will collaborate on driving reproducibility and expanding benchmarks to encompass emerging, complex AI workloads. Join us to share deployment insights and directly shape the benchmarking roadmaps guiding the next generation of supercomputing systems.

sess417.d: MPICH is one of the most widely used open-source implementations of the MPI standard and the foundation for many vendor MPI libraries powering today's HPC systems. This BoF brings together MPICH developers, industry partners, and HPC users to share the latest project developments, discuss support for emerging architectures and MPI features, and explore future directions for the MPI ecosystem. This year's session will also discuss opportunities for community engagement and contributions to MPICH. Attendees are encouraged to participate in an interactive format, ask questions, share experiences, and help shape the future of one of HPC's core software infrastructures.

sess413.d: Since SC25, a revolution has taken hold: coding agents have moved from curiosity into nearly every institution's pipeline, and "vibe coding" is now how much software, numerical included, gets written. That matters for numerical linear algebra (NLA), whose libraries underpin modern science and whose trustworthiness was built over 50 years of human expert engineering. Now, when a plausible NLA kernel is nearly free to generate, what holds that trust together? This BoF gathers established leaders and younger NLA scientists from academia and industry to open a discussion, so our community shapes this shift rather than being swept along.

sess408.d:
Open source has long been at the heart of HPC infrastructure management. Traditional HPC platforms have been well served by software stacks designed to meet this specific purpose.

A new era brings new demands for HPC and AI. Open source infrastructure management faces new challenges on many fronts.

This session features leading practitioners of a new generation of software-defined open HPC-AI infrastructure. The session will present a diverse range of open source solutions for current use cases, including advantages and disadvantages. Common problems will be identified and solutions shared. Attendees will be invited to share their experiences.

sess348.d: HPC computing centers face mounting procurement risks driven by geopolitical tensions, semiconductor supply constraints, and AI-driven demand for GPUs. Leading-edge fabrication is concentrated among a small number of fabs worldwide, leaving centers exposed when disruptions strike. What was once a predictable multi-year planning cycle has become a landscape of uncertainty. This BoF brings together center directors, vendors, and system integrators from across the international HPC community to develop shared adaptive strategies — from flexible RFPs to extended machine lifetimes. Community participation is central: the goal is not to deliver answers, but to build them together.

i: French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission, Directorate of Military Applications (CEA-DAM)

sess410.d: Quantum computing is experiencing accelerating transitions, from noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices to fault-tolerant quantum computers, and from quantum computers being objects of research to their becoming scientific computation tools. Quantum programming habits and assumptions must be revisited, and for the HPC community, this is more than an incremental hardware upgrade; it affects entire stacks. This session will explore how compilation workflows, execution models, and algorithmic strategies are expected to change to incorporate error correction and integrate with production HPC workflows. Thought leaders from the quantum industry, HPC, and academic research will exchange perspectives and engage the audience in discussion.

sess416.d:
Software has become central to all aspects of modern science and technology. Especially in high performance computing (HPC) and computational science and engineering (CSE), it is becoming ever larger and more complex while computer platforms evolve and become more diverse. Simultaneously, the teams behind the software are becoming larger, more technically diverse, and more geographically distributed. AI tools add both great potential and significant caution.

This BoF will address these issues and more, sharing experiences and best practices, and building community around software topics. Presentations and discussion notes will be made available at the BoF series website (http://bit.ly/swe-cse-bof).

i: NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR)

sess411.d: With power being a first-order design constraint on par with performance, it is important to measure and analyze energy-efficiency trends in supercomputing. To raise the awareness of greenness as a first-order design constraint, the Green500 seeks to characterize the energy efficiency of supercomputers for different metrics, workloads, and methodologies. This BoF discusses trends across the Green500 and highlights from the current Green500 list. In addition, the Green500, Top500, and Energy Efficient HPC Working Group have been working together on improving power-measurement methodology, and this BoF presents updates that will improve ease of submission without compromising accuracy.

i: Energy Efficient High Performance Computing Working Group (EE HPC WG)

sess385.d:
Several (trans-)national initiatives have recognized the crucial importance of co-design between hardware, software, and application stakeholders in the path to exascale and beyond. However, these regional efforts are somehow disconnected while the community would benefit by sharing return of experience, common know-how, and advancing on the new problems arising as exascale machines become more and more available.

The International Post-Exascale (InPEx) Project will bring together researchers and engineers, companies, funding bodies, and policy organizations to contribute to the implementation of an international, shared, high-quality computing environment based on the principles and practices of co-design.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory, University of Manchester

sess409.d: Ultra Ethernet has emerged as a major effort to create a scalable, open networking architecture for both AI factories and high-performance computing systems. As AI clusters continue to grow while HPC workloads demand ever-higher communication performance and efficiency, many networking requirements are beginning to converge. This BoF provides a forum for researchers, system architects, operators, application developers, and network vendors to discuss experiences, emerging requirements, unresolved challenges, and future directions for large-scale networking. The discussion aims to identify common needs across HPC and AI and foster collaboration toward open, interoperable networking solutions for next-generation computing systems.

sess376.d:
HPC infrastructures are being reshaped by rapid hardware innovation, pressure for greater energy efficiency, and the rise of AI and data-intensive workloads. Simultaneously, future directions are influenced not only by scientific communities and public research agendas, but also by industry roadmaps and emerging QC ambitions.

This BoF will examine how different countries plan future public HPC investments, how priorities are set, and who has influence in that process. The aim is to better understand whether public HPC remains community-driven or is increasingly shaped by industrial and market forces, and what this means for the future of research infrastructures.

sess269.d: This fireside chat explores neurodiversity within the HPC community. Join speakers from Microsoft and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory as they discuss workplace interactions, mentorship, and vital resources for neurodiverse individuals.

sess459.d:
High performance computing (HPC) and quantum computing are coming together to enable hybrid workflows that combine classical and quantum resources within a single computing environment. As quantum technologies evolve at different paces, integrating them into HPC systems introduces challenges for software, hardware, and scientific applications.

This panel brings together perspectives from HPC centers, quantum hardware development, and academic research to examine how HPC–quantum integration is approached in practice. Panelists will discuss software and systems layers enabling hybrid execution, including programming models, workflow orchestration, and middleware connecting HPC environments to quantum resources.

Drawing on early integration efforts, the discussion will highlight how communities are engaging with hybrid workflows — from deploying and evaluating quantum resources within HPC facilities to developing hardware and exploring algorithms and use cases. Panelists will share insights into challenges such as latency, resource management, as well as differing expectations around performance, usability, and readiness across quantum paradigms.

sess452.d: This panel will discuss the role of agentic AI and ML in the predictive science setting, with a focus on impacts to computational science and HPC. In particular, questions related to trustworthy agentic AI for science will form the core theme, as enabled by explainability and interpretability methods, as well as robust treatment of uncertainty in models and data. What are the particular challenges and opportunities for agentic workflows for modSim at exascale? How can uncertainty quantification be a scaffold for scientific AI/ML, and what are the pitfalls? This discussion will lay the foundation for future work in HPC co-design at the interface of theory, software, and hardware optimization as we prepare for new paradigms of predictive modeling and simulation in the era of agentic AI.

sess429.d: Software engineering is changing rapidly as AI-assisted programming becomes accepted. Tools and approaches have matured rapidly from “vibe-coding” to using complex and highly productive agentic harnesses. In this session, we will discuss the implications for the scientific programming community, with a particular focus on HPC software. This includes systemware, middleware, and tools used to operate, manage, and maintain HPC systems, as well as parallel simulation and modelling software used in HPC settings. Topics include trustworthiness and validation for AI-generated software, career futures and professional implications for systems engineers and research software engineers, security implications, and emerging current "best performance practices."

i: EPCC at the University of Edinburgh
US Association of Research Software Engineers

sess423.d: As quantum computing matures, challenges with the adoption of this technology shift from theoretical feasibility to practical deployment within established supercomputing infrastructures. This BoF examines the holistic framework required to operationalize quantum systems, from the physical datacenter floor requirements to the high-level application layer. We dive into the complex interplay between infrastructure installation, platform requirements, security protocols, and the necessary evolution of the software stack to support quantum algorithms and hybrid QC-HPC workflows. As such, this BoF outlines a strategic blueprint for building resilient, high-performance quantum-classical hybrid computing environments suitable for next-generation scientific discovery.

sess421.d: Continuum computing (digital continuum) is a distributed ecosystem spanning edge devices, scientific instruments, cloud platforms, data centers, supercomputers, and quantum systems. As these infrastructures become increasingly complex, agentic AI offers new opportunities for intelligent orchestration of computation, data, workflows, and heterogeneous resources. This BoF will explore how collaborative AI agents can enable autonomous scientific computing while ensuring trust, resilience, and human oversight. Topics include multi-agent coordination, AI-driven resource management, autonomous workflows, foundation models for scientific computing, and new programming models. The session will identify key research challenges and foster cross-disciplinary collaboration to advance the next generation of intelligent continuum computing.

sess399.d: A recent surge in novel AI accelerator hardware has sparked intense interest in running HPC applications and driven algorithmic research on these architectures. However, the maturity levels of associated tooling and software stacks vary significantly, with gaps in documentation and support. This BoF aims to explore trends in AI accelerators for HPC, ideal programming models, software stack support, code portability, training resources, and common challenges. We hope to foster a community of users interested or experienced in using AI accelerators for HPC applications.

i: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

sess431.d: While modern management platforms like OpenCHAMI streamline cluster orchestration, they do not inherently provide the comprehensive monitoring and data collection required to observe every facet of a next-generation data center. Operating heterogeneous, large-scale systems requires a unified, open-source observability framework capable of aggregating distributed logs, metrics, and traces across thousands of bleeding-edge compute nodes. This BoF session brings together HPC systems engineers, data center architects, and site reliability engineers to discuss the architecture, integration challenges, and best practices for building robust telemetry pipelines around OpenCHAMI, ensuring operational visibility, rapid fault isolation, and open-source compliance in next-generation supercomputing environments.

sess425.d:
RISC-V is an open standard instruction set architecture (ISA) enabling the open development of CPUs and a shared software ecosystem. There are already over 30 billion RISC-V cores, which are accelerating rapidly. Nonetheless, for all the successes that RISC-V has enjoyed, it is yet to become popular in HPC. Recent advances, however, such as data center RISC-V-based CPUs and PCIe accelerators, mean that this technology is becoming a more realistic proposition for our workloads.

This BoF aims to connect the RISC-V and HPC communities. We will explore how the technology is progressing and identify lessons learnt from previous years' predictions.

sess422.d:
As HPC enters an era of extreme heterogeneity and AI integration, user support is a critical strategic enabler. However, rising system complexity and finite staffing strain traditional models. To thrive in the AI and exascale era, a collaborative community approach is essential.

This BoF session invites practitioners, providers, and users to collaboratively reshape HPC support. Featuring insights from facility leaders on managing rapid AI adoption, an interactive live survey, and open group discussions, participants will share experiences regarding scaling, AI automation, and knowledge transfer. Outcomes will form a post-conference report dedicated to fostering a sustainable, community-driven support ecosystem.

sess420.d:
Open MPI continues to advance portable, high-performance communication for increasingly heterogeneous, accelerator-rich systems and workloads. Over the past year, the community has advanced MPI-5.0 conformance, expanded accelerator support, improved collective performance, and worked with partners across the HPC ecosystem. We'll discuss what Open MPI has accomplished over the past year and present a roadmap for the next year.

One of Open MPI's strengths lies in its diversity: we represent many different viewpoints across the HPC community. To that end, many developers from the community will be present to discuss and answer your questions both during and after the BoF.

sess419.d:
Emerging scientific needs are driving a new class of workflows that require near real-time processing, urgent computing, and time-sensitive decision-making. The traditional "compute-store-analyze" paradigm, which relies on dumping massive datasets to file systems for post-processing, has become an unsustainable bottleneck. It introduces unacceptable latency, and often renders high-frequency data analysis practically impossible.

This BoF discusses this challenge by exploring the architectural shift from file-based workflows to high-performance streaming. In this new paradigm, storage is treated not as a buffer for post-processing, but as a sink for final scientific results, while analysis, visualization, and reduction occur in-transit or in-situ.

i: National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC)

sess427.d:
The increasing computational demands are driving the deployment of ever-larger HPC and AI infrastructures. While these systems deliver unprecedented performance, they also pose critical challenges to their efficient use, particularly in terms of energy consumption.

This BoF will explore dynamic resource management as a key enabler of higher utilization and reduced energy consumption. Instead of traditional batch scheduling, dynamic resource control at the start or during a job’s runtime enables better allocation of compute capacity, memory, network availability, and storage. This BoF will address the two major key challenges of novel scheduling and its integration across the software stack.

sess432.d: The U.S. National Science Foundation's vision and investment plans for cyberinfrastructure (CI) are designed to address the evolving needs of the science and engineering research community. Senior leadership and program staff from NSF’s Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure (OAC) will discuss OAC's vision, strategic and national priorities, as well as highlights from the latest funding opportunities across all aspects of the research cyberinfrastructure ecosystem. Substantial time will be devoted to audience Q&A between attendees and NSF staff and unstructured time to meet informally with NSF staff.

sess424.d: Computer architecture simulators are central to exploring the design space of modern high-performance hardware and analyzing its performance. Many open-source simulators exist, targeting different hardware scopes, granularities, and metrics, yet none is perfect: issues with speed, accuracy, and usability limit their effectiveness for architecture researchers, accelerator designers, hardware-software co-designers, and performance engineers, among others. This BoF convenes an expert panel of users and developers from academia and industry to discuss these tools' shortcomings and possible responses. We invite all who build, use, or depend on these simulators to join the discussion and identify impactful community efforts, with outcomes shared publicly.

i: Erlangen National High Performance Computing Center (NHR@FAU)

sess350.d: Scientific AI on leadership-class HPC sits at the intersection of three concerns the community usually addresses separately: energy efficiency, uncertainty quantification (UQ), and verifiable trust. Compression and quantization change model behavior in ways that matter for scientific validity. Energy optimizations can quietly erode privacy and safety properties. And the HPC, UQ, and AI-safety communities rarely meet in one room. This BoF session brings them together to identify shared challenges, gaps in current practice, and concrete next steps toward AI systems for science that are simultaneously efficient, uncertainty-aware, and verifiably trustworthy on the world’s largest computing systems.

i: Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul

sess430.d: This BoF aims to build on the successful launch at SC25 of a multi-national community of practice. This year we focus on the Genesis Mission and DOE’s American Science Cloud and AI Models Consortium projects, to include establishing best practices for multi-facility or multi-institutional workflows, lessons learned from international contexts, sharing and accessing resources, developing mixed public/private partnerships, and protecting sensitive data privacy and security. Our goal is to advance progress in developing secure and trustworthy infrastructures for AI and integrated science. We seek to understand trustworthiness in supercomputing environments from both technical and socio-technical perspectives.

i: DOE Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research
DOE Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research

sess428.d: HDF5 has anchored HPC I/O for 25 years, and AI-driven science is redefining what "trustworthy data at scale" demands: verifiable provenance, concurrent I/O, and cloud-native interoperability. Short talks from domain scientists launch interactive segments where an opt-in agentic survey captures attendee priorities, pain points, and open questions in real time, with aggregate results used to steer the discussion. This session is for seasoned HDF5 developers and domain scientists, and anyone just starting out or wondering what HDF5 is about: bring the problems you'd like to solve, and help steer the discussion and provide input to future HDF5 roadmap planning.

sess418.d: Energy consumption has become a key constraint in high performance computing (HPC), shaping system design, procurement, software, and scientific workflows in the exascale era. As large-scale simulations and AI-driven workloads increase power demand, the community must reconsider how performance is measured, optimized, and reported beyond FLOPs alone. This BoF session will convene researchers, facility operators, vendors, and application scientists to discuss energy measurement, performance-per-watt metrics, efficient algorithms and runtimes, workload scheduling, and carbon-aware computing. The session will identify practical gaps, share lessons from production systems, and define community priorities for sustainable, energy-efficient HPC at scale.

i: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
Energy Efficient High Performance Computing Working Group (EE HPC WG)

sess453.d:
Quantum computing is increasingly being integrated into HPC environments, yet its impact on scientific discovery, especially in combination with AI workflows, remains limited by a more fundamental challenge: usability. Today’s hybrid quantum–HPC–AI workflows are fragmented, manually assembled, and difficult to reproduce, requiring users to navigate multiple abstraction layers, toolchains, and system constraints. At the same time, the user base is expanding beyond quantum experts to domain scientists who require intuitive, reliable, and scalable workflows.

This panel examines how to move from access to impact by focusing on the design of user-centered quantum–HPC–AI workflows. Drawing on perspectives from scientific computing, data workflows, system design, and applied research, panelists will explore workflow bottlenecks, abstraction strategies, orchestration challenges, and the role of AI. The discussion will focus on what is required to make hybrid systems usable in practice and how to translate emerging capabilities into measurable scientific productivity.

sess460.d:
As agentic AI and dynamic dataflow models increasingly dominate modern compute landscapes, monolithic architectures struggle to maintain optimal cost-performance ratios. This panel explores the heterogeneous disaggregation of AI workloads, addressing the critical systems-level challenges of orchestrating complex models across diverse, next-generation accelerators.

Panelists will discuss the evolution of software infrastructure, alongside advanced scheduling strategies required to manage dynamic execution and cost-aware SLAs. By decoupling memory, compute, and networking, we can achieve highly efficient, scalable execution in fragmented environments. Join experts as they debate the future of hardware-software co-design, evaluate marginal cost-efficiency trade-offs across contemporary AI hardware, and outline the system software innovations necessary to fully realize the potential of disaggregated infrastructure at scale.

sess454.d:
Quantum computing has often been integrated with HPC systems as an add-on: scheduled through custom adapters, monitored through bespoke hooks, bolted onto facilities as parallel infrastructure. This reflects how most sites operate today, but it stops short of deep integration and does not provide the right foundation for the decade ahead.

The alternative view holds that quantum and HPC should be designed as one holistic system from the start, with quantum resources running through the same schedulers, workflow engines, and observability systems already in place. SC26 arrives at an inflection point: nine DOE national laboratories are actively deploying quantum systems, IBM has published its Quantum-Centric Supercomputing reference architecture, and DOE has launched the $293 million Genesis Mission targeting quantum-AI-HPC convergence. The systems are going in. This panel asks how to design that integration correctly from day one rather than assembling it as a series of bolt-ons.

sess461.d: AI-driven workloads are outpacing what any single institution can afford, power and cooling constraints are tightening, and the workforce required to support next-generation HPC is in short supply. Regional collaboration is increasingly proposed as the answer — but does it actually work? This panel directly confronts that question. Drawing on operational experience from national HPC centers, regional networks, and campus research computing programs, panelists will debate the economics of cost-sharing, the governance challenges of federated infrastructure, and the realities of shared staffing and data management. Informed by the March 2026 NSF-CASC Workshop on NAIRR regional hubs and PEARC community discussions, the panel is structured as a moderated debate designed to surface genuine divergence/agreement and drive toward actionable insight for institutions making long-term infrastructure decisions right now.

sess457.d: Quantum processors are not useful in isolation. Today's small-scale QPUs require only modest classical hardware, but as systems scale toward utility and fault tolerance, dependencies on classical HPC and AI grow rapidly. These dependencies span the full stack: real-time decoders for fault-tolerant error correction, AI-assisted state preparation and circuit synthesis, hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, HPC-scale data processing, and verification. The serious questions for the SC community span all timelines: Which applications can quantum-HPC-AI integrated systems meaningfully accelerate now, which become reachable with fault tolerance, and which remain infeasible despite widespread touting? Integration approaches differ widely — RIKEN's Fugaku-IBM/Quantinuum hybrid platform, DOE lab user programs at NERSC and ORNL, NVIDIA's NVQLink GPU-QPU interconnect, and Google and AWS's standalone fault-tolerant roadmaps with classical co-processing serving error correction. These distinct framings reflect different visions for HPC-AI integration, and our community lacks consensus on which application and architecture pairings are optimal.

sess455.d: To cement their legacies, a group of HPC luminaries have generously volunteered to be replaced by AI. They have kindly agreed to provide expert responses to prevalent chatbot queries regarding HPC, thus generating natural-intelligence content for AI training. We must acknowledge, however, that our experts may have ulterior motives regarding some topics, and we must take steps to avoid data poisoning. We need audience participation from people like you to detect and label fallacious content!

sess149.d: The landscape of AI for science has shifted dramatically. Beyond building ever-larger models from scratch, the scientific community is increasingly leveraging powerful pre-trained models — adapting them through fine-tuning, domain specialization, and integration into complex AI systems combining reasoning models, knowledge graphs, agentic workflows, and connections to simulators and instruments. These shifts highlight a full stack of interdependent challenges for developers, scientists, and HPC centers, from strategies and infrastructure for sharing data and computing, to frameworks orchestrating multiple models and agents, to methods and tools for ensuring safety, alignment, and rigorous evaluation of scientific reasoning and skills. Progress in any one area both depends upon and accelerates the others. This workshop will highlight advances across this interconnected landscape, emphasizing openness, international collaboration, and community-driven efforts, featuring peer-reviewed papers and invited talks spanning shared infrastructure, open model development, agentic AI systems for science, evaluation and safety, and driving challenge applications.

i: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Japan

sess151.d: Interactivity enables the exploitation of HPC in new and revolutionary ways, delivering many new and exciting opportunities for our community. Interactive HPC involves users being in the loop during job execution monitoring a job, steering the experiment, or visualizing results to make immediate decisions. Likewise, urgent computing combines interactive computational modeling with time-sensitive systems in the real world such as the near-real-time analysis of unfolding disasters to inform real-time decision making. Supporting interactive and urgent workloads on HPC requires expertise in a wide range of areas and the solving of numerous technical and organizational challenges. This workshop brings together stakeholders, researchers, and practitioners from across interactive and urgent computing within the wider HPC community. We will share success stories, case studies, and technologies to continue community building around leveraging urgent and interactive HPC as an important tool for scientific research, responding to disasters, and addressing societal issues.

i: French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA)
National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC)

sess155.d: This workshop brings together HPC researchers, operators, and vendors from around the globe to present and discuss state-of-the-art HPC system testing methodologies, tools, benchmarks, procedures, and best practices. The increasing complexity of HPC architectures and growing need to leverage HPC for integrated workflows demands more extensive testing than ever to evaluate the status of the system after installation or software upgrades and ensure operability before it is transitioned to production. Different methodologies are used by HPC centers and vendors to evaluate systems during their lifetime, not only at the beginning during installation and acceptance, but also during maintenance and alongside regular operations. This workshop provides a venue to present and discuss the latest HPC system testing technologies and methodologies. The event will include an opening talk focused on current HPC system testing topics, followed by a series of paper presentations from peer-reviewed accepted submissions, concluding with a panel discussion.

i: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)

sess154.d: RISC-V is an open standard instruction set architecture (ISA) which enables the open development of CPUs and a shared common software ecosystem. There are already over 15 billion RISC-V cores, which are accelerating rapidly. Nonetheless, for all the successes that RISC-V has faced, it is yet to become popular in HPC. Recent advances, however, such as data center RISC-V-based CPUs and PCIe accelerators, mean that this technology is becoming a more realistic proposition for our workloads. This workshop aims to connect those currently involved in RISC-V with the wider HPC community. We look to bring together RISC-V experts with scientific software developers, vendors, and supercomputing center operators to explore the advantages, challenges, and opportunities that RISC-V can bring to HPC. Furthermore, we aim to further expand the RISC-V HPC SIG, enabling interested attendees to participate in one of the most exciting open-source technological activities of our time.

sess148.d: Scale to See: Scalable AI for Scientific Imaging and Spatiotemporal Data is a half-day workshop at SC that brings together researchers at the intersection of high performance computing (HPC), artificial intelligence (AI), large-scale scientific imaging and spatiotemporal data. Scientific imaging and spatiotemporal data — from climate and earth systems to medical imaging, materials science, and cosmology — are increasingly high-dimensional, multimodal, and time-evolving, demanding AI methods that are not only accurate but also scalable, physics-aware, and deployable on leadership-class HPC systems. This workshop focuses on AI methods and systems explicitly co-designed for extreme scale, including HPC-aware model architectures, scalable training and inference pipelines, physics-integrated learning algorithms, and efficient computing techniques for high-dimensional data. Through peer-reviewed papers, invited talks, and panel discussions, the workshop aims to set a research agenda, foster interdisciplinary collaboration, and build a community around AI that operates natively at HPC scale to transform scientific imaging and spatiotemporal analysis.

sess157.d: Providing a sustainable path for supercomputing is a pressing topic for our community, industry, and governments. Supercomputing has an insatiable appetite for computational cycles, while we face increasing challenges of delivering performance per Watt advances with silicon technology trends. All within the context of the converging needs of HPC and AI, climate change, the drive towards net-zero, and economic pressures driven by geo-political challenges. Improving the sustainability of supercomputing provides many opportunities when the end-to-end cycle is considered. From the design of computational circuits and systems; to the power and cooling that is used to operate them, along with the suite of software tools used to administrate, maintain, and raise operational efficiency of HPC systems, with the increasing pressures from the AI aspects being added to traditional HPC workload and workflows. All elements of the system considered, from compute nodes and interconnects to IO and storage components of the system.

i: EPCC at the University of Edinburgh

sess156.d: High performance computing (HPC) is decentralizing into a sensor-edge-cloud continuum. Modern edge AI pipelines for perception and control now face the same systemic bottlenecks that define supercomputing: data-management overhead, interconnect topology, and accelerator utilization. This workshop on Edge-Cloud-HPC Operational Continuum (ECHO) applies an HPC lens to resource-constrained environments, investigating how foundational principles must evolve for non-deterministic edge and cloud infrastructures. We focus on three pillars: (1) exporting HPC rigor to the edge through hierarchy-aware parallelism, co-designed memory management, and high-performance streaming I/O; (2) reclaiming predictability for cloud-native HPC by mitigating virtualization overheads, multi-tenant resource contention, and stochastic provisioning; and (3) expanding HPC influence into adjacent domains, including Edge/IoT, MLOps, and cyber-physical systems via shared metrics, reference workloads, and reproducible benchmarking that reports variance and tail behavior. We invite papers, experience reports, and demos, and we encourage artifact packaging for comparison.

sess150.d: The inherent wide distribution, heterogeneity, and dynamism of the current and emerging high-performance computing and software environments increasingly challenge cyberinfrastructure facilitators, trainers, and educators. The challenge is how to support and train the current multidisciplinary users and prepare the future educators, researchers, developers, and policymakers to keep pace with the rapidly evolving HPC environments to advance discovery and economic competitiveness for many generations. The 13th annual full-day workshop on HPC training and education is an ACM SIGHPC Education Chapter coordinated effort, aimed at fostering more collaborations among the practitioners from traditional and emerging fields to explore educational needs in HPC, to develop and deploy HPC training, and to identify new challenges and opportunities for the latest HPC platforms. The workshop will also be a platform for disseminating results and lessons learned in these areas and will be captured in a special edition of the Journal of Computational Science Education.

i: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Lincoln Laboratory

sess152.d: Accelerators are now a central component of modern HPC systems, delivering an increasing share of computational capability and enabling tightly coupled, highly heterogeneous node architectures. This evolving landscape — spanning GPUs, AI/ML accelerators, FPGAs, dataflow devices, and emerging quantum processors — creates both new opportunities and significant challenges in algorithm design, performance portability, and programming model standardization. WACCPD 2026 brings together researchers and practitioners working on programming models, compilers, runtimes, and applications for accelerator-based systems. The workshop focuses on approaches that enable performance, scalability, and portability across diverse architectures, including directive-based models, standard language parallelism, portable frameworks, and task-based and data-centric systems. It also highlights mixed-precision techniques, AI-assisted programming, and hybrid classical–quantum workflows. Through peer-reviewed papers, invited talks, and a panel, WACCPD fosters exchange of ideas and showcases methods and case studies that advance programmable, sustainable, and high-performance heterogeneous computing.

sess153.d: Operational data analytics (ODA) provides unique opportunities to analyze, understand, and optimize HPC operations. Readily available open-source frameworks make the collection of telemetry from different operational domains of HPC increasingly easy. However, analyzing the data, extracting actionable knowledge from it, and leveraging it to optimize HPC operations is challenging. While most HPC sites have sophisticated monitoring capabilities in place, their analysis capabilities often do not go beyond visual inspection by humans via dashboards or static thresholds for alarms. Few early adopter sites have pioneered advanced usage of data, but its wider adoption will depend on success stories and the availability of analysis tools and models. This workshop will bring together HPC users, practitioners in HPC operations, monitoring experts, and data analytics researchers to share experiences, discuss state-of-the-art research, and foster collaboration. It will solicit papers with concrete, reproducible, and empirical data gathered through case studies, research for practice, and surveys.

sess458.d: For decades, computing drew on a shelf of demonstrated, but undeployed, technology, stocked largely by government-funded research. HAMR, the technology now carrying the HDD roadmap, came off that shelf: a 2001 federal cooperative agreement co-funded its early development; volume shipment arrived two decades later. The government funding instrument retired in 2007 on the premise that industry would restock the shelf. In magnetic data storage, where few suppliers face few hyperscale buyers, that premise collapsed into a vertical market failure, with suppliers rationally declining to fund breakthrough R&D. Buyers feel the consequences in shortages, rising prices, year-long lead times, and missed technology roadmaps. Demonstrated technologies sit unfunded, and the market still lacks a tier combining tape's low cost with quick access. The panel debates whether this stall threatens other computing technologies and closes on two ways to restock the shelf: pooled and matched pre-competitive investment, and AI demand for near-storage processing.
